client: I've been really struggling this past week with this big presentation I have coming up at our annual conference. Yesterday during practice I just completely blanked — forgot everything I'd rehearsed — and now I can't stop thinking about it happening again in front of everyone. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help, because the presentation is next week and I feel like I'm running out of time.
therapist: That sounds really exhausting — carrying that moment of blanking around with you all week, and feeling the clock ticking at the same time. I notice you mentioned you're not sure talking will help, and I'm curious about that — what would feel most useful to you right now, even if it's just a small step forward?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, fast speech

client: Honestly, I'm not even sure what a small step forward would look like right now. Like, the presentation is in two weeks and my mind just goes blank every time I try to practice, and I end up sitting there feeling worse than when I started. I guess what I want is to just... not feel so panicked about it, but I don't know if talking through it actually makes that happen.
therapist: It makes a lot of sense that you'd question whether talking helps when what you really want is relief from that panicked feeling — that's such an honest thing to name. What you're describing, where practicing actually makes things feel *worse*, often happens when our mind is so focused on catching itself failing that it can't access what it already knows. Can you tell me a little more about what goes through your head in those moments right before you blank — is it more of a thought, like "I'm going to mess this up," or more just a physical wave of dread?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: It's more like a physical wave first, honestly — my chest gets tight and my mind just goes blank before I even have a chance to think anything. But then the thought comes rushing in after, something like "everyone can see you're falling apart" or "you're proving you don't belong here." It's like the dread hits first and then my brain piles on to make it worse.
therapist: What you're describing — the body sounding the alarm before your mind even has a chance to respond — is actually really common with performance anxiety, and those thoughts that follow, like "I don't belong here," can feel so convincing in that moment even when they aren't true. I'm struck by how clearly you can map that sequence out, which tells me a part of you already has some distance from it. I'm wondering — when that thought "you don't belong here" shows up, does any part of you push back on it, even quietly?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Honestly, sometimes there's this tiny voice that goes "wait, you've done this before, you've gotten through it" — but it's so quiet compared to the other one. It's like trying to hear someone whisper across a loud room. And then I feel almost guilty for not being able to hold onto that quieter voice, like I should be stronger than this by now.
therapist: That quieter voice is real, and it's actually telling you something true — you *have* done this before, and that matters. The guilt you're adding on top, this idea that you "should be stronger by now," is really just the loud voice finding a new angle to pile on, and you don't have to accept that framing. What do you think that quieter voice would say if it had the whole room to itself?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess... if that quieter voice had the whole room, it might say something like "you've gotten through hard nights before, and you're still here." But honestly, even as I say that, I feel kind of embarrassed, like I'm just telling myself a feel-good story to avoid the real truth that I'm not handling my anxiety as well as I should be at this point in my life. It's hard to trust that voice when the louder one has so much more... evidence, I guess.
therapist: The way you said that — "you've gotten through hard nights before, and you're still here" — that's not a feel-good story, that's actually evidence too, just the kind the loud voice conveniently ignores. I'm also noticing there's something tender in how you're talking about this, like you're being careful with yourself even while criticizing yourself, and I wonder if the embarrassment you feel about that quieter voice is itself worth looking at. What would it mean about you if that voice were actually right?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That question kind of stops me in my tracks, honestly. Like, if that quieter voice were actually right, it would mean... I'm not as broken as I think I am? And I don't know why that feels almost scarier to believe than the harsh stuff, but it does.
therapist: What you just said — that believing you're *not* broken feels scarier than the harsh stuff — is one of the most important things you could notice about yourself, and it takes real courage to say it out loud. Sometimes the critical voice feels safer because it's familiar, and hope can feel risky because it means something could actually change. I'm sitting with that with you — what do you think makes it feel dangerous to believe you might be okay?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I think... if I let myself believe I might be okay, then I have to actually try. Like, if I'm broken, there's a reason things don't work out, a reason I stay home instead of reaching out to people — but if I'm not broken, then the loneliness is kind of my fault, and that's terrifying. It's easier to have an excuse than to risk trying and still ending up alone anyway.
therapist: What you just uncovered is really profound — the "brokenness" has been quietly protecting you from the risk of trying and still being hurt, and that's not weakness, that's actually a very human way of keeping yourself safe. But I notice as you said it, there was something in your voice that sounded almost fragile, like this truth is both a relief and a weight to carry at the same time. Can you sit with this for a moment — what would "trying" actually look like for you, in the smallest, safest way you can imagine?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I think... trying might look like just texting one person I used to be close to, someone I've been avoiding because I'm scared they've moved on without me. But even as I say it out loud, my chest gets tight, because what if I reach out and they don't respond, or worse, they respond but it's just polite and distant? I guess that's the thing — the "smallest, safest way" still feels like standing at the edge of something really high up.
therapist: That image of standing at the edge of something high up — that's such an honest way to describe it, and it tells me you're not minimizing how real this fear is. What strikes me is that you already know *who* you'd reach out to, which means part of you has been holding onto that connection even while avoiding it. I wonder — what would you need to tell yourself in that moment of hitting send to make it feel like a step worth taking, even with the uncertainty of what comes back?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess what I'd have to tell myself is that the silence I'm already living with is worse than whatever response I might get back. But honestly, even saying that out loud feels a little hollow, because part of me doesn't fully believe it yet. Like, what if I reach out and they're just... polite about it, and I can tell it's not real, and then I feel even more alone than I do now?
therapist: The fear you're naming — that a polite but hollow response might hurt more than silence — is so real, and it makes complete sense that the words feel a little hollow when the belief hasn't fully caught up yet. Belief usually follows action in small steps, not the other way around, so you don't have to fully believe it before you try. I'm curious — when you imagine the version of you who does send that text, what does that person look like on the other side of it, regardless of what comes back?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I guess that version of me... feels a little less like I'm just waiting around for someone to notice I exist. Like maybe I took up some space instead of just shrinking back again. But honestly, it's hard to picture that person clearly because I've talked myself out of sending that text so many times that it almost feels like the not-sending is just who I am now.
therapist: The way you said that — "the not-sending is just who I am now" — landed quietly, like something you've almost made peace with but haven't quite. And yet the image you found, of taking up space instead of shrinking, that's not nothing — that's you describing something you actually want, even if it feels far away right now. What would it mean to you to reclaim that as part of who you are, rather than leaving it as something the not-sending took from you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech
